questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Several aspects of my motivation were rather crucial. Academical opportunities to explore the subjects chosen and being able to combine them with my background at UCPH as a Geography student is especially important to me. However, there is also the fact that biogeography is different everywhere you go, and as such, getting a taste for more of it in a different continent and place from what I've seen so far in my life is something I will not just go by.

Besides these things, however, I also have a taste for traveling the world and exploring new cultures and their people. As I was feeling somewhat at an impasse in my life, it also came to be something that has helped me overcome the depression I fell into during autumn last year, and knowing myself, I knew that if I got to be thrown into a new place and life to be for a while, I would (and have) feel much better.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It wasn't easy at all to be frank. As I only had the final confirmation of my stay abroad in late December (and left on January 5th), I had to arrange everything both here and there in a very short time frame, and thus also found myself very much overwhelmed with figuring out sometimes even basic things that if given the proper time and such to arrange it would've been a breeze. Luckily, I very quickly got in contact with several key personnel from York University there who could help me in all aspects - especially that of ensuring I was properly admitted to my classes and what not.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Like mentioned in the above question, I received a lot of help especially from the study leaders of both Environmental Science and Geography, Ann and Anne, without whom I would not have made it far in navigating everything. But also my fellow students and classmates would ensure I got fit well in nicely with all technicalities and overall just a good welcome.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were options for living on both campuses, and I lived on the French campus of Glendon. And although all my classes were at the other campus, there was good options for transport both publicly and a shuttle specifically for students to go back and forth every day.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a meal plan available that you had to take, so it was mandatory. I personally found that I missed my kitchen a /lot/ during the stay as you have zero cooking facilities unless you can prove your need for one medically, which I probably could have considering my allergies, but the hassle of it was big, so I did not bother as I don't need to avoid too many of the usual day-to-day items.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
The fact that there's not really a cooking option is a thing. But although it is hard to be creative when you do not eat meat, it is still doable.
Consider your options. If I had stayed for longer, I probably would have found some off-campus housing quickly after settling properly, but when you're there for a short time, it's quite okay and a good way to also meet many good friends in campus housing! But regardless, you actually most often meet people when you have a specified place to study, such as the breezeway of Glendon Campus, where I spent countless hours studying, which is quite surprising.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was alright for our purposes. It wasn't great, but it was nice to have something that's nice and actually affordable ready for you when you come. If in doubt about things, just call and talk with general people around, if there's one thing to note about the Canadians it is their hospitality :-)

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process was very complicated due to several factors - for one, the host institute changed the time of the stay from the fall to the spring semester. Secondly, I received my final "acceptance" for this change very late in December, and thus I had already in fact prepared my life around not going at all in the spring semester, which led to a whole array of complications not only in regards to the stay and what not, but also because of my life, my apartment and what not back home. So I had a very stressful Christmas to say the least.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not a whole lot. Luckily, my friend and I were both going to the same host university, so we could help one another with everything from ensuring each other's to-do lists, and also just figuring things out. The contact that was assigned to us from UCPH was, unfortunately, answering neither their emails, phone calls or anything else in regards to helping out in the unique circumstances that I was in.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As the time of the semester changed from fall to winter, I was, unfortunately, unable to get the exact classes I originally applied for that had a heavy emphasis on field studies and related things. So naturally due to Canada's local climate, there are no field trip courses in the winter semester. But besides that, after a direct conversation with my study leader at York University, I was able to enroll in exactly the courses I wanted to do, which helped me immensely.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get in direct contact with the advisors and such over there personally as soon as you can, it will help you a lot more compared to simply wreaking through the things on your own.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I picked four courses that all had a very high workload, and as such when I got corona over there and fell sick, I knew immediately I had to cut one down despite having already completed some 40% of said course. Overall, my courses were focused around biodiversity and biology, but still with biogeography as its core. But for someone who did not even have biology in high school, it was a lot of hard work to get into courses that were specifically for fourth year biologists, which in turn for me personally led to me learning a lot academically as I was being challenged constantly, but could also for some mean major setbacks.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style was incredibly different. At home, we are used to studying at our own pace fully until the exams, then we show up and 100% of the grade is dependent on the exam, which can be both a lot, but also means less stress during the semester overall. At York, however, there are constant deadlines that all have a minor influence in your grade, and this can add up to your workload a lot if you're also just trying to learn the basics of things as well besides it. It took a lot to get used to this type of learning, but I am also grateful at my resolve in going through it properly.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Biogeography. Biodiversity. Ecology & conservation Science.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The above courses are specifically catered to someone like me who has an interest in both biology and geography. But there are a multitude of courses that I feel the future exchange student is better suited to figuring out what works for them specifically.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Corona testing at the time I needed it was very expensive over there.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food. Although I knew there was a meal plan that I needed to have, I did not think food would be as expensive as it was. Although it could have been worse than what I spent. I would have been capable of preparing much better, and more nutritious foods at a much lower cost on my own compared to the canteen foods.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There's a multitude of sports, club activities and more you can be involved in. I found myself in a lot of different activities with my fellow students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I doubt I can cater to all interests in that regard.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Get a bit out of Toronto as well. But also ensure that you get to see what the city has to offer overall that you can be part of.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was quite alright, although there are some differences, it was easier to find similarities with people, and I found myself quite liking the culture and work ethic that the Canadians possess.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Smile and greet the world!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I mostly found a lot of them peculiar or funny, to be honest. One of my good friends there has a knack for apologizing at things that is no one's, and least of all their fault, which I found very entertaining as it was something that pertains to a lot of Canadians. But overall, it's really just about finding that common ground and recognizing that all people are different no matter the cultures they're from.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I personally found the welcoming attitude of the Canadians to be the greatest thing about it all. No matter when or where, they will find the time to stop and talk with you on a personal level, even if you're only meeting them by chance for the very first time!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Firstly, it is important to recognize that to do things, in general, is a little expensive over there. So it is important to ensure your financial stability, but also that it's okay to use the money for things that add value.

Academically, you will most likely be working individually for most of your courses and items, which can be a challenge to some. Although there is group work as well, all important things rely on your ability to personally structure and prepare all your own things and to see ahead.

Go see some Ice Hockey! And various other sports! These kinds of things are a craze over there, and it is awesome! I very much regret the fact that I'm such a klutz on the ice myself compared to what I could have been, and seeing them definitely did not make that better, but that's alright!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not a lot beyond what is already described. Keep an open mind and get out of your comfort :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To me, I would highlight the fact that you get to expand your network all around, which is also a big part of my life as a university student and part of what I believe it is to work at this level of education and type of education I possess so far and continue to study - my networking is not purely contained within Copenhagen or Denmark as a whole, but rather the whole world, which I believe adds a lot to my perspectives.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The short deadline with which I had to prepare properly was by far the biggest obstacle to me alongside getting corona shortly before the exam period.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
